- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially after spikes.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model underestimates; increase early-term forecasts to capture downward momentum.
- Model often overshoots in the first 5–7 days after a price spike; apply a 3–5 day decay filter to smooth out overreaction.
- If sentiment history shows strong reversal (e.g., from positive to negative), model fails to adjust; apply a mean-reversion penalty to forecast mid-term.
- For 30-day horizons, model frequently underestimates true volatility; scale up forecast variance when sentiment is erratic or mixed.
- When sentiment is flat or neutral (0.33–0.67), model tends to lag; add a 1–2 day lead-in adjustment to anticipate slow-moving trends.
- Avoid forecasting extreme values (e.g., >5.0 or <0.5) unless sentiment strongly supports it; cap or floor forecasts based on sentiment intensity.
